articles.title: 'Couldn't even fill single Ramlila Maidan': BJP's Nitin Nabin takes jibe at Rahul's 'vote chori' rally
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: BJP national president Nitin Nabin on Monday targeted Congress leader Rahul Gandhi over his 'vote chori' allegations, claiming the INDIA bloc
articles.body: NEW DELHI: BJP national president Nitin Nabin on Monday targeted Congress leader Rahul Gandhi over his 'vote chori' allegations, claiming the INDIA bloc had failed to fill even a single Ramlila Maidan during its rally in Delhi. Addressing a BJP rally in Karimnagar, Telangana, Nabin said BJP workers had drawn larger crowds across more than 200 locations and accused Rahul of advocating for alleged infiltrators to be included in voter lists."Rahul Gandhi ji used to say that vote chori took place. Rahul ji, the people are with us, and the votes are with us. The people of Karimnagar have shown that their blessings are with us. They (the INDIA alliance), despite putting in their all, couldn't even fill a single Ramlila Maidan, while BJP workers gathered far more people than could fit in a Ramlila Maidan at over 200 locations," news agency ANI quoted him as saying.Nabin also questioned Rahul Gandhi's claim that 13 crore votes had been stolen and challenged his stand on the inclusion of people whose whereabouts were allegedly unverified."Rahul ji claimed that 13 crore people's votes had been stolen. But I would like to ask: Why should 3 crore people be included in the voter list? More than 6 crore people have shifted. I know that in Telangana, lakhs of people have shifted their votes. So, should people be allowed to vote twice? The remaining 3 crore are those whose whereabouts the Election Commission enquired about in 2003, but they have no answers. So, the person advocating for these 3 crore infiltrators is none other than Rahul Gandhi," he said.Nabin targets INDIA bloc over vote theft allegationsThe BJP chief accused opposition parties of attempting to create chaos, while asserting that the BJP was receiving public support through democratic means."They tried to spread chaos—let them have their chaos! We, on the other hand, are receiving democracy's blessings," Nabin said.Taking a swipe at Rahul Gandhi's references to the Constitution, he said, "I have come to tell those who carry a copy of the Constitution around in their hands: you have a copy of the Constitution in your hands, but the Constitution is in our hearts. You speak of the Constitution, but we revere it. That is why we respect all constitutional institutions."He also invoked the Emergency to target the Congress, saying, "The people who murdered democracy by imposing the Emergency to save their own seats are today invoking democracy."Nabin also criticised Rahul Gandhi's remarks on India's economy, accusing him of insulting the country both within India and abroad."Whenever Rahul Gandhi is in the country, he does nothing but insult it, and he insults it abroad too. Rahul ji goes everywhere saying that India's economy is a disaster. Rahul ji, India's economy and its development are advancing on a global scale. Today, India has moved beyond the Fragile Five to become the world's fourth-largest economy," he said.Expressing confidence about the BJP's prospects in Telangana, Nabin said the party would hold the state government accountable."I am sure the countdown to the Telangana government has begun. BJP karyakartas will now hold the Telangana government accountable," he said.He also predicted that Prime Minister Narendra Modi would return to the Red Fort in 2029."Modi ji will not go anywhere; he will appear on the ramparts of the Red Fort again in 2029. Rahul ji, keep dreaming. India's youth, farmers, women, workers and people from every section of society stand with PM Modi. PM Modi is going nowhere. He will return to the ramparts of the Red Fort in 2029. Rahul ji, keep dreaming! The youth, farmers, women, workers and every section of Indian society stand with PM Modi," he said.Nabin's Telangana visit was part of the BJP's 'Loktantra Bachao, Arajkata Hatao' campaign. The party has launched the campaign to counter what it describes as attempts by Congress and other opposition leaders, particularly Rahul Gandhi, to mislead people through fear, confusion and misinformation.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Quote of the Day by Robert Frost, "A mother takes twenty years to make a man of her boy, and another woman makes.."
articles.summary: Robert Frost is one of the most beloved poets of America. He wrote poetry that people grew up reading, poetry that was impactful and relatable.
articles.body: Robert Frost is one of the most beloved poets of America. He wrote poetry that people grew up reading, poetry that was impactful and relatable. Frost was known for his crystal clear descriptions of rural life, nature, human relationships and the complex nature of the human mind, as he converted seemingly simple moments into reflections on life, love, loneliness, choices and mortality. His poetry was easy to understand, but incredibly deep in meaning. He was one of the most widely read and respected poets of the 20th century.His works often included country roads, snowy woods, stone walls, farms and quiet talks. But these familiar images hid questions about human existence, individual freedom, responsibility and the choices that shape our lives. His poetry was timeless because it linked the natural world with human feelings.Early life and educationRobert Lee Frost was born in San Francisco, California, on March 26, 1874, the son of William Prescott Frost, Jr., a journalist and teacher, and Isabelle Moodie. His father named him after the famous Confederate General Robert E. Lee. Frost was raised in California for his early childhood, but his father died of tuberculosis in 1885 and his mother took him and his younger sister to Lawrence, Massachusetts to be closer to his father's parents.The transition was difficult and the loss of his father hit him hard. Yet during his school years there was an early interest in literature and writing. He developed a taste for poetry and an interest in the works of classical and contemporary writers.Frost graduated from Lawrence High School in 1892, sharing the position of class poet with Elinor White, his future wife. He attended Dartmouth College and later Harvard University, but did not finish at either. He was more interested in pursuing his own intellectual and creative interests than in following a conventional academic path.In 1895 he married Elinor White and the two began a life together that would bring both happiness and considerable personal tragedy.The struggle before recognitionFrost did not achieve literary success overnight. For years he was a teacher, a farmer and a writer, trying to find his footing. He and his wife lived on a farm in Derry, New Hampshire, where he was close to rural life. These years became an important inspiration for his poetry. His experiences as a farmer gave him a close acquaintance with nature, with the changes of the seasons, with the work of the fields, and with the relation of man to his surroundings. Rather than romanticising rural life, Frost often depicted its difficulties, isolation and emotional complexity.Disillusioned by the lack of recognition in America, Frost moved in 1912 with his family to England. This choice was important for his literary career. His first book of poems, A Boy's Will, was favourably received when it appeared in 1913. His second collection, North of Boston, published in 1914, made him known as an important new poetic voice.It included some of his best known poems, such as Mending Wall and After Apple-Picking. In 1915 Frost came back to the United States and his work began to attract a good deal of attention.His writing style and popular worksFrost’s greatest contribution to poetry was his ability to make the common experience address universal human concerns. His language was conversational, his settings familiar and his characters often common people. But his poems had layers of meaning, making the reader think beyond the story itself.One of his most famous poems, The Road Not Taken, published in 1915, is about choices and their consequences. Another famous work, Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening (1923), describes a traveller stopping to admire a forest in the snow. In Mending Wall, Frost meditates on the walls we erect between ourselves as humans. The poem is about the tension of tradition and change, it asks why human beings put up barriers when they may no longer be of any use. His poem Birches meditates on childhood, imagination and the wish to escape the hardships of life. Fire and Ice deals with destructive human emotions through contrasting images of desire and hatred. Frost often employed nature as a metaphor for human experience. His woods, his roads, his trees, his seasons were not merely descriptions of scenery. They were about loneliness, and uncertainty, and hope, and conflict, and the passage of timePersonal tragedies that shaped his thoughtFrost's life was not without deep personal suffering. He lost many members of his family, including his parents and some of his children. His daughter Marjorie died in 1934 from complications of childbirth and his son Carol died by suicide in 1940. His wife Elinor died in 1938. These experiences brought sorrow and emotional trauma to his life. To put all the dark elements in his poetry down to personal tragedy would be simplistic but his writing often showed an awareness of human vulnerability, loss and the uncertainties of existence.What set Frost apart was his refusal to provide pat solutions. His poetry spoke to the possibility of beauty, the possibility of pain, living side by side and the necessity of making hard choices at times without knowing where they might lead us.Awards, impact, and contribution to literatureFrost won four Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry (1924, 1931, 1937 and 1943) and is one of the most distinguished American poets of his generation. He was asked to read his poem The Gift Outright at the inauguration of President John F. Kennedy in 1961. The bright sunlight made it difficult for him to read the poem he had prepared, but he recited another poem from memory, displaying his extraordinary command of his work.Frost inspired generations of poets and readers in demonstrating how poetry could address philosophical questions within the framework of simple narratives and everyday experiences. His works are still taught in schools and colleges around the world.Robert Frost died January 29, 1963, in Boston, Massachusetts, at the age of 88.Quote of the DayOne of the most famous quotes of Robert Frost is, "A mother takes twenty years to make a man of her boy, and another woman makes a fool of him in twenty minutes." It is a witty yet thought provoking observation on the influence of love, upbringing and human emotions on a person’s life. At first glance it seems to be a humorous remark on the romantic influence of a woman ruining a mother’s years of sacrifice. But behind the humour is a deeper commentary on how easily people can lose their judgement when emotions take over.The first part of the quote glorifies motherhood and the painstaking process of raising a child. It takes patience, sacrifice and countless little lessons to turn a young boy into a responsible man. Most of this influence is quiet, in the form of daily acts of caring, encouragement and example.The second part introduces a comic contrast. His comment about another woman making a fool of him in twenty minutes is indicative of how quickly romantic attraction, infatuation or the desire to impress someone can cloud judgement. A man who has spent years learning to think for himself can act irrationally when he falls in love. He could ignore the advice of common sense, act on impulse, neglect his priorities, or do things that he would normally think were stupid. In these moments, reason can be overcome by passion.But the quote is not to be read as women being blamed for men’s bad choices. The point is deeper: human vulnerability. It's wonderful what attraction and love can make a sensible person do. It also contrasts the slow, gradual process of character-building with the sudden intensity of emotions that can sometimes test it.These words hide another interesting thought. Upbringing provides us with the basis to make good decisions but growing up also means learning to exercise that judgement independently. It is not the values you are taught that test your character, it is whether you can hold on to those values when tempted, attracted or pressured emotionally.Finally, Frost reminds us that it takes years to build character, but a moment can be enough to lose one's sense of perspective. It's a funny reminder that no matter how much wisdom we acquire on the way to growing up, we need to learn to bring it along when emotions get involved.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Bangladesh garment workers' protest: Manufacturers set to propose 15% wage hike; offer likely to be rejected
articles.summary: Bangladesh's garment manufacturers are expected to propose a roughly 15% hike in the minimum monthly wage of protesting workers during talks with
articles.body: Bangladesh's garment manufacturers are expected to propose a roughly 15% hike in the minimum monthly wage of protesting workers during talks with authorities on Monday, Reuters reported, citing industry leaders.However, the proposed increase falls well short of workers' demand for a monthly minimum wage of 30,000 taka ($242), more than double their current pay of 12,500 taka ($101). According to labour representatives, workers are unlikely to accept an increase significantly below their demands.Industry leaders argued that a wage hike exceeding 15% would be "unsustainable" for the garment sector, which is facing rising costs and weak global demand."Even then, many small factories could struggle to cope with the increase," one industry leader said.Meanwhile, labour unrest continued on Monday, with protesters forcing dozens of garment factories to shut down in Ashulia and Gazipur, two major apparel manufacturing hubs on the outskirts of the capital, Dhaka.Factory owners have warned that the unrest could further disrupt production and export shipments during a crucial period for overseas orders.Why are Bangladesh's garment sector workers protestingWorkers in Bangladesh's garment sector have been protesting since early November, demanding higher wages amid rising living costs. The unrest has triggered factory shutdowns and violent clashes in the world's second-largest garment-exporting nation, which employs more than 4 million (40 lakh) people in the sector and supplies major global retailers, including H&M, Gap, and Walmart.The wage dispute threatens to undermine the cost advantage of an industry that accounts for more than 80% of Bangladesh's export earnings.According to a survey by the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association, disruptions over an 18-day period caused losses of around $428 million across 317 factories. International buyers also shifted orders worth approximately $254 million to other countries amid concerns over production disruptions.Industry leaders say rising production costs, higher utility tariffs and intense competition from rival garment-producing countries have limited manufacturers' ability to accommodate a substantial wage increase.The protests, which began earlier this month, forced hundreds of factories to shut down and triggered clashes between workers and police. Security forces used tear gas and sound grenades to disperse demonstrators.Global labour groups back workers' wage demandsSeveral global labour rights organisations, trade unions, and brand coalitions have thrown their support behind Bangladeshi garment workers' demands for higher wages.On November 19, the Action, Collaboration, Transformation (ACT) initiative, a global wage-bargaining platform bringing together apparel brands and trade unions, called for an urgent and meaningful increase in the country's minimum garment wage, citing rising living costs, inflation, productivity and prevailing economic conditions.In a joint statement, ACT also expressed concern over reports of violence and retaliation linked to the wage-setting process, urging all parties to respect workers' rights to freedom of association, peaceful assembly and social dialogue.The initiative further called on the government-appointed wage board to reach a negotiated settlement that would bring workers' pay closer to a living-wage level.ACT's brand members, including H&M Group, Inditex, C&A, Primark, Next and PVH Corp, said they would work with suppliers to ensure that statutory and negotiated wage increases were reflected in purchasing prices.You use AI every day. articles.summary: RAIPUR: Chhattisgarh state consumer disputes redressal commission in Raipur has partly allowed cross-appeals filed by The Oriental Insurance Company
articles.body: RAIPUR: Chhattisgarh state consumer disputes redressal commission in Raipur has partly allowed cross-appeals filed by The Oriental Insurance Company Limited and a contractor, modifying a district commission order in a theft claim involving two excavators.The bench of president justice Gautam Chourdiya and member Pramod Kumar Verma pronounced the order on November 4.The appeals challenged a May 20, 2026 ruling by the district consumer disputes redressal commission, additional bench, Raipur, which had directed the insurer to pay Rs 1,03,51,000 towards the insured declared value of an excavator (Rs 52,51,000) and another excavator (Rs 51,00,000), along with Rs 5 lakh for mental and physical distress and Rs 20,000 for litigation costs.According to the record, the contractor insured the two excavators from September 27, 2022 to September 26, 2023 and from November 9, 2022 to November 8, 2023 respectively under contractor’s plant and machinery floater policies.The contractor stated that the machines broke down on August 26, 2023, were parked about 800 metres off the road near Tandul village close to Rakhi police station in Raipur district, and were repaired with a mechanic.The operator left for his native village amid rain for two to three days, and when the contractor returned on August 28, 2023, the machines were missing.The contractor submitted a written request for a theft report at Rakhi police station on August 28, 2023 and complained to the senior superintendent of police in Raipur on August 29, 2023 after the police station did not register a report.Following a judicial magistrate’s order dated Oct 24, 2024, police registered an FIR and later filed a closure report.The insurance company contended that the complaint was time-barred, the machines were in transit rather than at the project site, the owner left them unguarded, and the absence of tyre or chain marks raised suspicion.The state commission rejected those articles.title: Iran's Fereydun Plan to defy US blockade: 14 tankers ready for showdown, Gulf oil facilities at stake
articles.summary: Iran is preparing to test the waters with the United States, with Tehran reportedly planning a major oil tanker operation to challenge Washington's naval
articles.body: Iran is preparing to test the waters with the United States, with Tehran reportedly planning a major oil tanker operation to challenge Washington's naval blockade.The move could bring Iranian vessels directly into confrontation with American warships, as Tehran warns that any attempt to attack or stop the convoy would trigger retaliatory strikes on oil infrastructure across the Persian Gulf.According to a report by The Jerusalem Post, citing satellite imagery, vessel-tracking data and Iranian media reports, Tehran is preparing a convoy of more than 14 oil tankers to challenge the US naval blockade.The vessels are reportedly gathering near Kharg Island, Iran's principal crude oil export terminal, and are expected to head towards the Gulf of Oman. The report said the tankers have been assigned crews and are flying Iranian flags, signalling a possible attempt by Tehran to move its oil shipments despite Washington's restrictions.Kharg Island handles around 85 to 90 per cent of Iran's crude oil exports, making it central to the country's efforts to resume shipments. However, there has been no official announcement from Tehran confirming the convoy's departure.The reported tanker operation comes amid a proposal circulated by Iran's hardline media to break the American blockade.According to The Jerusalem Post, Iran's IRGC-affiliated Fars News Agency published a column outlining what has been described as the Fereydun Plan, which calls for Tehran to send a group of oil tankers through the US naval blockade rather than allow Washington to dictate Iran's oil exports.The proposal takes its name from Fereydun, a legendary figure in the Persian epic Shahnameh. Drawing a parallel with his story of crossing a river despite being denied passage, the column argued that Iran should demonstrate its ability to move oil shipments despite American restrictions."To break the naval blockade, Iran can move a group of tankers that will break through," the Fars column stated.The proposal further suggests that Tehran should warn Washington against attacking or detaining the tankers, threatening retaliation against energy infrastructure in the Gulf if American forces attempt to stop the convoy. Similar proposals have also appeared in Iranian publications Hamshahri Online and the Young Journalists Club.The warning accompanying the proposed tanker operation is particularly significant, as Iran-linked media have threatened retaliatory strikes on oil infrastructure across the Persian Gulf if American forces attack, intercept or stop the convoy.The Fereydun Plan specifically identifies oil facilities in the United Arab Emirates as potential targets. Iranian media reports have also referred to energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, raising the possibility that a confrontation at sea could spread to critical oil installations across the region.The proposal warns that any American attempt to prevent Iranian tankers from passing could invite retaliation against the energy facilities of countries supporting Washington's blockade.You use AI every day. articles.title: Punjab's security nightmare: Guns from Pakistan, shooters from within, elections ahead
articles.summary: CHANDIGARH: Punjab is heading into an election year with a security problem that has outgrown its border villages.
articles.body: CHANDIGARH: Punjab is heading into an election year with a security problem that has outgrown its border villages. Over the past few months, the same fence has let through an AK-47, M16 rifles, Glock pistols and a rocket-propelled grenade, along with more than half of India's seized heroin. Six policemen have been shot dead this year, some on duty, some inside their own outposts, one on his way home from the gurdwara. The most recent was found in uniform near a Gurdaspur bypass last Sunday.What links these events is less a movement than a model. Security agencies point to Shahzad Bhatti, a Pakistan-based gangster-turned-terrorist working at the behest of the ISI, and to an outfit called Tehreek-e-Taliban Hindustan (TTH) that claims attacks on social media.Handlers abroad find recruits online: a young man with a criminal streak, a woman whose husband is in jail on a drug charge, a teenager who wants quick money. They pay for small "test tasks", ask for the video, and escalate to violence. Drones deliver the weapons. Anyone who is arrested is cheap to replace.The network is not confined to Punjab either. A railway blast in Rajasthan, a plot against police in Delhi and a car bomb in Haryana have all been traced back to it, or to the same method.However, experts are wary of calling it a revival of the Khalistan movement. Defence analyst Ajai Sahni describes the violence as largely mercenary, feeding on gangster networks and on the vulnerable. But with assembly elections due in early 2027, motive may matter less than momentum. Agencies are watching whether a steady drip of attacks can become something bigger once campaigning begins, and what that would mean for candidates, party workers and the vote itself.This story traces how that pipeline works, from the border to the phone screen to the trigger.Since February this year, Punjab has witnessed six murders of policemen. The latest victim was head constable Vinod Kumar, 42, whose blood-soaked body, still in uniform, was found near a Gurdaspur bypass last Sunday. Police said that they were investigating a social media claim by an outfit --Tehreek-e-Taliban Hindustan (TTH) -- taking responsibility for the killing. TTH has made similar claims before, for at least two earlier killings of policemen.Intelligence and law enforcement agencies say that one man is behind TTH’s propaganda and operations: Shahzad Bhatti. A Pakistan-based gangster-turned-terrorist, Bhatti, as described by Indian agencies, is working at the behest of the ISI. Investigators say his method is consistent. He recruits cheap local hands online, pays them for small “test tasks”, and has them film what they do.Punjab shares a 553km border with Pakistan, and its assembly elections are due in early 2027. As campaigning nears, the weapons seizures, the drone drops and the attacks have all picked up.How Shahzad Bhatti’s name entered the pictureBhatti’s name surfaced in a string of cases across northern India.In January, a car packed with gas cylinders and explosives was parked inside the premises of Baldev Nagar police station in Ambala, Haryana, and blew up. In July, the National Investigation Agency chargesheeted eight accused, Bhatti among them. The agency said he had recruited and radicalised the seven arrested Indians through social media and encrypted channels. It also said some of the accused had videographed the scene for “dissemination and publicity”.In April, the Gujarat ATS detained one Bikramjit Singh alias Vicky in Deesa town. He is accused in a Punjab grenade-smuggling case and was working as a labourer at a roadside restaurant, allegedly under a concealed identity. The ATS said he disclosed links to Bhatti and his associate Abid Jutt, and that he recruited Punjab youths for the network.Then came Delhi. This summer, the Delhi Police Special Cell arrested five alleged members of a multi-state module linked to Bhatti, in a coordinated operation across Delhi, Haryana, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh.The accused are Sohail (26), Sonu Meena (30), Sachin Kumar Meena (20), Mohammad Kaif (21) and Mohammad Rihan (20). Police say three other members of the same module had been arrested earlier.According to police, the group had a clear brief: target police personnel, spread extremist propaganda and recruit young people. They were allegedly told to carry out reconnaissance of police stations and security camps, arrange weapons, and paste posters and graffiti promoting TTH across the Delhi-NCR region. Officials noted that TTH had recently claimed responsibility for the killing of an assistant sub-inspector in Punjab’s Amritsar district.Each accused had a role:Sohail painted TTH graffiti at several locations in Delhi and Faridabad and shared videos with his handlers.Sonu Meena arranged weapons and provided financial help.Kaif and Rihan were tasked with recruiting youth, scouting security establishments and planning attacks.Police also claimed that Rihan had been offered Rs 3 lakh to carry out a firing attack on police personnel.Five firearms, ten live cartridges, posters linked to the network and videos allegedly used to track and threaten police personnel were seized.A senior officer put it plainly: TTH is a front driven by Bhatti with the strategic backing of the ISI.Defence expert Ajai Sahni says the threat is widening beyond a single handler. “There is an increasing mix of Pakistan-backed players, such as Shahzad Bhatti, Khalistani sympathisers and local gangsters. They act largely under the influence of Pakistan and, to some extent, of extremist elements in the Sikh diaspora, particularly in Canada, the US, the UK and a number of other countries.“Take Shahzad Bhatti: he has gained significant traction through his social media presence over the past two to three years, and that is why he holds some sway over gullible youths who have a penchant for landing on the wrong side of the law. Since there is clearly some degree of sympathy towards Khalistan, players like Shahzad Bhatti are ready to exploit it at the drop of a hat, as people like him enjoy clear patronage and money flowing in from Pakistan,” Sahni ponders.For Punjab, the Delhi arrests were a warning, not a comfort. TTH, the outfit the Delhi module was allegedly promoting, had just claimed the killing of an ASI in Amritsar’s Majitha, so a network built to terrorise police in Delhi-NCR is also being tied to attacks inside Punjab. It also shows the cost of this model. Recruits are paid small sums, and some are offered lakhs for a firing attack, while the handler sits in Pakistan. That makes it cheap to replace anyone who is arrested. With policemen already being shot, arms and drugs coming across the border in growing quantities, and elections approaching, each new recruit gives the network another way to strike a state that is already under strain.The weapons pipelineThe quantity and sophistication of recovered weapons are what worry Punjab’s police most.In June, the BSF seized an AK rifle, 25 pistols, 47 magazines, 368 rounds and a light bulletproof jacket. A BSF source said the jacket points to preparations for a strike, because such protective gear is rarely found in routine smuggling cases. In August, Tarn Taran Police and the BSF recovered an MP-9 rifle and seven pistols, including four Glocks.October and November brought more:October 4: Amritsar Rural Police busted a Pakistan-linked module and recovered an AK-47 and two grenades. Police said the weapons had been pushed in by drone.October 10: An M16 rifle, nine pistols and 15 kg of opium were recovered, and four people were held.November 10: Police recovered a rocket-propelled grenade, a drone and two pistols in a joint operation with a central agency. Separately, Amritsar Commissionerate Police recovered 14 pistols and arrested six people.November 17: Amritsar Rural Police seized ten pistols and 102 cartridges alongside the heroin haul.The problem goes beyond the numbers. Pistols such as Turkish-made Ziganas are reaching small-time criminals and willing teenagers, not just trained militants. Drones deliver them across the border, and police say they usually find out only after a recovery or an attack.The drug floodThe same border and the same drone routes carry narcotics. The NCB’s latest report shows how large the problem is. Punjab accounted for 2,086kg of heroin seized in 2025, which is 58% of the national total of 3,567kg. Drone-related cases rose from three in 2021 to 305 in 2025, and Punjab accounted for 298 of the 305.A June, 2026 TOI report also flagged a “second wave” of pharmaceutical opioids, with 8,95,508 bottles of codeine-based cough syrup seized in the state, the highest in the country.Investigators have not publicly tied the heroin to Shahzad Bhatti. They do describe the same pattern, though: foreign-based handlers, drones and local couriers. On November 17, Amritsar Rural Police seized nearly 39kg of heroin along with the pistols and said the accused were in touch with such handlers. On October 14, the BSF caught a Punjab Police constable, posted with the state’s own anti-drone system, with 15 kg of heroin in his car.Narcotics money and weapons smuggling feed each other. The same networks that sell heroin can sell guns, and the profits can pay young recruits to do the shooting.Politics, a 'double-edged sword'Sahni says the roots of the problem lie in politics. “Things are always controlled from the top down, and at the top is always the political leadership. Every political party in Punjab plays a double game when it comes to Khalistani sentiment and drugs.“They do not take a hard line but rather engage in soft double-speak. Although the police have arrested several people linked to drugs and gun violence, no big fish has ever been caught. To put it plainly, we must first eliminate political involvement and patronage, because organised crime is collusive. Supply matters, but only when demand carries equal weight.”The playbook: honey traps, cash and 'test tasks'If the weapons are the hardware, recruitment is the software.On November 3, a blast damaged the Anupgarh-Suratgarh railway line in Sri Ganganagar, Rajasthan. Investigators say a Pakistan-based ISI handler known as “Shah” ran the operation. Rajasthan ATS arrested two people from Gurdaspur, Mahakdeep Kaur, 21, and Devendra Singh, 22.Officials say Kaur was lured through a reverse honey trap: romance, money and the promise of a better life offered online. They say she came into contact with Shah after her husband was arrested in a drug trafficking case. The two accused allegedly received Rs 2.23 lakh. Their first visit to the site on October 6 and a second attempt failed, and the blast came on the third visit. ATS chief Dinesh MN said the handler wanted to spread panic in Sri Ganganagar and across Rajasthan. Investigators analysed nearly five lakh call records and questioned over 400 people to trace the accused.Officials say it fits a larger pattern. Pakistan-based operatives target lonely women online, assuming they will attract less suspicion. After Operation Sindoor, intelligence assessments showed a rise in social media recruitment by Pakistani operatives. The ATS draws parallels with Jaipur resident Babita Dhankar, arrested in June for alleged links to terror outfits across the border.Shah and Bhatti are separate names in the investigations, and no official link between them has been stated publicly. The method looks the same, however: online grooming, small payments and tasks escalating from “tests” to violence.Why Sri Ganganagar rings alarm bells for PunjabSri Ganganagar in Rajasthan shares a border with both Pakistan and Punjab, and the trail from the Nov 3 blast led straight back to Gurdaspur. The two accused are from there, and Punjab Counter Intelligence helped trace them. For poll-bound Punjab, that is the warning: a handler across the border can use local recruits to hit targets in a neighbouring state, and the same network can turn back to Punjab at any time.‘Mentoring’ young men into attackersThe Delhi cases show how an escalating task works. After Sohail’s graffiti job, the Special Cell arrested three youths who were in direct contact with Bhatti, Jatt and Gujjar. Bhatti allegedly told them to record videos showing firearms and to film themselves shooting a policeman, with hefty rewards promised.The three tracked a Uttar Pradesh Police personnel and filmed the chase. They tried to open fire, but their country-made pistol jammed. When the policeman turned around, they fled, and the Special Cell caught up with them. Officials say the case shows what the network wants: killings of police personnel, filmed and circulated as propaganda.Not every plot fails. In April, a suspected bomber was killed when an IED went off prematurely as he planted it on the freight corridor in Patiala. Four members of the module were arrested within 12 hours. Police said the module’s alleged kingpin was in contact with a Malaysia-based pro-Khalistan terrorist and Pakistan-based arms suppliers. That blast, which police called low-intensity, was the second attack on Punjab’s freight corridor this year. A January explosion near Sirhind injured a loco pilot and derailed a goods engine.Policemen in the crosshairsPunjab Police personnel have been the main targets this year. The list so far:February 22-23: ASI Gurnam Singh and homeguard Ashok Kumar killed inside a police outpost in Gurdaspur, close to the border.May 24: ASI Joga Singh gunned down near Majitha.September 11-12: ASI Jaswant Singh survived after a bullet grazed his head.September 18: ASI Harjit Singh killed on PCR duty in Amritsar.Early October: GRP ASI Sukhchain Singh wounded in Ajnala.October 11: ASI Iqbal Singh shot dead in Tarn Taran on his way home from the gurdwara.November 15: Head Constable Vinod Kumar found shot dead in Gurdaspur.Why the timing worries PunjabLook at the last two months, and the intensity stands out. October and November together include the Tarn Taran and Amritsar arms recoveries, the 39kg heroin haul, the RPG recovery, the Sri Ganganagar railway blast and the Gurdaspur killing.Agencies are watching the same question. As campaigning intensifies, can the network turn a steady drip of attacks into something bigger? Heavy weaponry and killings of people in public life have already raised concerns about the security of candidates, party workers and the electoral process.Sahni urges caution on how to read the violence. “Election-related violence is not new in India, but because Punjab is a border state, it poses a far greater risk, not only to the state itself but also to national security. Even so, it is too early to call this a revival of the Khalistan movement, because the recent incidents are not ideologically driven. They are mainly mercenary in character, exploiting the existing networks of gangsters, as well as personal vulnerabilities, such as drug addicts or the poor..”Punjab Police point to their record: crackdowns involving joint nakas with the BSF, 109 suspects apprehended in an ongoing drive and dozens of recoveries. The state installed its own anti-drone system along the border last August. Yet when a constable posted with that very system is caught carrying heroin, the problem is plain to see.‘Manufactured grievances’Sahni cautions against reading the crisis as a problem of poverty alone. “To link this to poverty alone would be unwise. The real problem in Punjab is the progressive erosion of the quality of life. A major factor in it is the manufactured grievance that the Sikh community has not been given enough representation in politics, business and other important spheres of Indian society. These are manufactured grievances, and community members should not seek refuge in them.”With efforts underway to track other members of Bhatti’s modules, one reality is hard to ignore. The border is porous to drones and handlers can reach recruits online, so officials know the pistols, packets and propaganda videos will keep coming. The months before the vote are when that pressure will be hardest to contain.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chandigarh | Silver Rate in Chandigarh | Bank Holidays in Chandigarh | Public Holidays in Chandigarh | Chandigarh AQI | Weather in Chandigarh | Petrol Price in Chandigarh | Diesel Price in Chandigarh | CNG Price in Chandigarh | LPG Price in ChandigarhStay updated with the latest Chandigarh news. articles.title: US army seeks to proceed with 5-tonne chemical blast in Iowa despite court order halting detonation
articles.summary: The US Army is seeking to bypass a federal court order blocking its plan to detonate five tonnes of potentially dangerous explosive chemicals in Iowa,
articles.body: The US Army is seeking to bypass a federal court order blocking its plan to detonate five tonnes of potentially dangerous explosive chemicals in Iowa, arguing that delaying the operation could increase the risk of an accidental explosion as temperatures drop.Government lawyers urged the 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals to allow the Army to proceed with the operation, saying swift action was necessary to protect military personnel and nearby communities, according to an Associated Press report."Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay," the government lawyers said in a court filing late Saturday, adding that the Army wanted to carry out the detonation by Tuesday.The planned operation involves destroying 68 drums containing around five tonnes of lead azide, an explosive chemical used in the manufacture of munitions. The material was discovered in a deteriorating condition at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in March.A federal appeals court had earlier put the operation on hold after environmental groups challenged an emergency permit issued by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). The detonation was initially scheduled for Friday but was postponed to Monday following concerns raised by residents and elected officials.Why the Army wants to proceed with the explosionArmy officials have argued that the lead azide has become extremely unstable because of its deteriorating condition and could explode accidentally if handled or transported.According to officials, crystallisation of the chemical inside the drums has increased the risk of an uncontrolled explosion. They have warned that even slight friction or movement could trigger a blast, making relocation or alternative disposal methods potentially dangerous.Government lawyers also argued that falling temperatures could further destabilise the material, increasing the threat of an accidental explosion. They said temperatures in the region were expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 1 degree Celsius) in the coming days.The Army has maintained that a controlled detonation is the safest available option after consulting explosives experts, engineers and environmental safety specialists.However, environmental groups have questioned whether all possible alternatives were properly examined. They have also criticised authorities for failing to provide sufficient information to residents who could be affected by the operation.Residents fear lead contamination, health risksThe proposed explosion has triggered concerns among residents in and around Middletown, a small community in southeastern Iowa located about 160 miles from Des Moines.The Army has acknowledged that the detonation could release lead-containing particles into the air, forming a plume that could eventually settle on the ground.Lead exposure can cause serious health problems, and there is no known safe level of lead exposure. Residents have expressed concerns about possible contamination of farmland, crops, livestock, pets and nearby properties.Some residents have also been warned about potential damage to windows due to the noise and ground vibrations caused by the explosion.The Army had recommended that people in affected areas remain indoors, keep doors and windows closed, bring pets and livestock inside and clean outdoor surfaces after the operation. Residents were also advised to take precautions to prevent contaminated dust from entering their homes.Environmental groups, including the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, have called for greater transparency and a review of the emergency permit granted by the EPA.They argue that communities deserve more advance notice and clearer information about the possible consequences of the explosion.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Texas homeowner disputed State Farm's handling of storm damage after the insurer estimated repairs at $1,718.56, below her $2,698 deductible; a federal judge has sided with the company and dismissed her claims
articles.summary: A Texas homeowner who sought more than $61,000 to repair storm damage to her house has lost her legal battle against her insurance company.
articles.body: A Texas homeowner who sought more than $61,000 to repair storm damage to her house has lost her legal battle against her insurance company. Maria Garcia had challenged State Farm Lloyds after it estimated the covered repairs at just $1,718.56 and refused to pay, saying the amount was below her policy deductible of $2,698. However, a federal judge has ruled that Garcia failed to provide enough evidence to show that the February 2024 storm caused the additional damage for which she wanted compensation.The disagreement began after a storm hit Willacy County, Texas, on February 16, 2024, according to the information available in the ruling. Garcia contacted State Farm on the same day to report damage to her home. Her homeowners' insurance policy was active at the time and covered the period from June 8, 2023, to June 8, 2024.The insurer later examined the property on July 18, with Garcia present. Its inspection found some damage to the roof and sunroom. However, the company believed that several roof shingles had been damaged in earlier storms and had not been repaired. It therefore included only the damage it linked to the February 2024 weather event in its estimate.Garcia disagreed with the assessment and turned to Arroyo Construction and Maintenance for another inspection. The contractor put the estimated repair bill at $61,420.74, a figure far higher than State Farm's assessment. The two reports also differed over when the damage had occurred. This became a major issue in the case, as the insurance policy did not cover damage from storms that had taken place outside its validity period.The dispute eventually reached the US District Court for the Southern District of Texas. Garcia accused the insurer of failing to honour its policy and handling her claim unfairly. But on November 20, US District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. ruled in State Farm's favour and dismissed all five claims brought by her.Why State Farm rejected the repair claimState Farm's inspection identified damage to 36 roof shingles. However, it attributed 17 of them to an earlier storm in 2020, saying the damage had not been repaired. The insurer linked the remaining 19 shingles and damage to the sunroom to the February 2024 storm.After calculating the cost of these repairs, State Farm arrived at an estimate of $1,718.56. Since this was below Garcia's deductible of $2,698, the company declined to make a payment under the policy.Garcia challenged the assessment by submitting a report from Arroyo Construction. The contractor identified damage to the roof as well as water stains inside the house. It estimated that the necessary repairs would cost $61,420.74.However, the report did not establish that all the damage had occurred during the February 2024 storm. It noted that the weather event had brought rain and wind gusts approaching 40 MPH to the area. While the wind could have damaged the roof, the contractor also found signs of hail damage. No hail had been reported during the February storm, prompting the need for further investigation into the history of the damage.The contractor also linked the damage inside the house to another storm that had affected the McAllen area on April 21, 2023. That storm occurred before Garcia's insurance policy began.State Farm also submitted reports from an engineer and a contractor who examined the property. They said the roof damage could have resulted from several weather events over the years. Their reports referred to storms in August 2020, May and October 2021, and June 2023.Homeowner could not establish damage timingThe difference between the repair estimates was not enough to settle the dispute in Garcia's favour. The judge examined whether the evidence could establish that the February 2024 storm had caused the additional damage included in her claim.The court found that the reports did not clearly separate damage from the covered storm from damage caused by earlier weather events. Although the contractor had identified several problems with the property, its findings did not establish that the February 2024 storm was responsible for the additional repairs Garcia wanted State Farm to cover.This distinction was important because an insurance company is not automatically responsible for every problem found during an inspection. The homeowner had to provide evidence connecting the claimed losses to an event covered by the policy.The judge also considered Garcia's argument that State Farm had failed to investigate the claim properly. She pointed to the time taken between reporting the damage and the insurer's inspection, which took place about five months later. She also alleged that the company had underestimated the damage and failed to explain its decision adequately.State Farm maintained that the disagreement was about the cause and extent of the damage, rather than unfair treatment of its customer.The court found that Garcia had not produced evidence showing that the insurer acted unfairly or deliberately mishandled her claim. It also noted that, during her deposition, she had acknowledged having no separate complaints about State Farm's conduct beyond the disagreement over coverage.Judge rejects all claims against insurerGarcia's lawsuit included five claims. She accused State Farm of breaking the insurance agreement, violating consumer protection and insurance laws, acting in bad faith and failing to make payments within the required time.The judge rejected all five. The court found that Garcia had not established that she was entitled to additional insurance benefits under the policy. This also weakened her allegations that the company had violated insurance rules or failed to settle the claim fairly.Her allegations of misleading statements also failed. The court found no evidence that State Farm had made a specific false promise about the coverage available under the policy or that Garcia had suffered a separate injury because of any such statement.The judge further rejected her claim that the insurer had failed to make a timely payment. Since the evidence did not establish that State Farm owed additional money for the February 2024 damage, the court found no basis for holding the company responsible for delayed payment.In its November 20 order, the US District Court for the Southern District of Texas granted State Farm Lloyds' request for summary judgment. This meant the insurer won the case without a trial, with the court ruling in its favour on every claim Garcia had filed. Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. said a separate final judgment would follow.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Ro Khanna raises the issue of visa appointment backlogs, says none should have to choose between traveling to see a dying loved one and risking their ability to come back to US
articles.summary: US Congressman Ro Khanna raised the crucial visa issue that H-1B visa holders from India have been facing for the last 11 months.
articles.body: US Congressman Ro Khanna raised the crucial visa issue that H-1B visa holders from India have been facing for the last 11 months. They traveled to India and could not get a stamping appointment and could not return to the US for months. The issue became so serious that immigration experts advised visa holders against traveling outside the US as they might have jeopardize their chance to come back to the US. In a Facebook post, Khanna said visa delays were creating difficulties for workers who travel outside the US and are unable to return because of prolonged waits for visa appointments.“Visa appointment backlogs are leaving skilled workers stranded abroad for months, separated from their jobs and families,” Khanna wrote. He also highlighted the personal difficulties caused by the delays, particularly for people facing family emergencies. Without specifying the visa categories or the nationalities of the people who are facing this problem, Khanna wrote: “No one should have to choose between traveling to see a dying loved one and risking their ability to return home,” the California Democrat said.Khanna called on the State Department to address the delays and expand visa appointment availability.His remarks come amid continuing concerns over US visa appointment delays, which have affected foreign workers, including H-1B visa holders who travel abroad for visa stamping and face extended waits before they can return to the US. A September 2026 report by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) highlighted staffing shortages at US consulates as one factor behind prolonged nonimmigrant visa interview waits. The number of consular officers handling nonimmigrant visas fell from 1,342 in fiscal year 2024 to 904 in fiscal year 2025, amid hiring freezes and attrition.The State Department publishes monthly estimates of visa interview wait times and says additional appointment slots are released regularly. However, it cautions that the estimates do not guarantee an appointment within a specific period.The current crisis was triggered in December 2025 when social media vetting ws introduced for H-1B and H-4 visa holders. articles.title: Agnipath's new rules, Uttarakhand's old concerns: The road to 2027 assembly polls
articles.summary: Uttarakhand has long been a state where military service runs through generations.
articles.body: Uttarakhand has long been a state where military service runs through generations. From the hills of Kumaon to Garhwal, joining the armed forces has meant not just serving the country, but also securing a stable livelihood and a future for one's family.Now, as the state prepares for the 2027 assembly elections, the Agnipath scheme is set to become part of the political conversation. The Centre's November 4 decision to extend the service tenure of Agniveers from four to six years, with a pathway to permanent enrolment subject to selection criteria, has brought a significant change to the recruitment model introduced in 2022.The revision comes as the first batches of Agniveers approach the end of their initial four-year tenure. The Uttarakhand government has also announced measures, including reservation in certain state government jobs, to support those leaving military service.For the BJP, these changes offer an opportunity to address concerns surrounding the scheme. For the Congress, which has opposed Agnipath since its introduction, questions remain over long-term employment and the future of military recruitment.In a state where the armed forces occupy a central place in society, Agnipath is therefore more than a recruitment policy. As Uttarakhand heads towards the polls, the debate is shifting from what the scheme promised in 2022 to what its revised provisions can deliver in 2027.Why military service matters so much in UttarakhandIn Uttarakhand, military recruitment is more than a statistic. For generations, it has carried the promise of a better life. For many people in the isolated hills, military service creates a path out but not away.Joining the Army has traditionally offered young men a stable income, a recognised profession and the possibility of supporting their families. But military service is not just about financial security. It also carries social prestige, a sense of belonging and a tradition passed down through generations.This relationship has developed alongside Uttarakhand's longstanding employment challenges. Opportunities remain limited in many hill districts, while industries, educational institutions, healthcare facilities and transport infrastructure are concentrated in the plains and urban centres.Migration, therefore, is not driven by unemployment alone. Families also move in search of better education, healthcare and infrastructure. For villages already experiencing population decline, the departure of young people further weakens local economies.Military recruitment has offered a route out of economic uncertainty without necessarily requiring people to abandon their connection to the state. While it cannot solve Uttarakhand's employment challenges, it remains an important part of its social and economic fabric.This is where the Agnipath scheme comes into play. It has changed the terms of a career that many families traditionally regarded as a dependable route to long-term security.Agnipath's revised rules and what they mean for recruitsWhen the Centre introduced Agnipath in June 2022, it replaced the earlier system of regular military recruitment below officer rank with a four-year tenure. Only 25 per cent of recruits could be retained permanently, based on merit and organisational needs, while the remaining 75 per cent would exit with a lump-sum Seva Nidhi package, but without pension or long-term benefits.The government presented the reform as a way to build a younger, tech-ready military while reducing pension costs and preparing disciplined talent for the civilian workforce. Critics, however, questioned whether a lump-sum payout and military training could substitute for a secure career, particularly in Uttarakhand, where recruitment exam paper leaks and cancellations have added to employment concerns.On November 4, 2026, the Centre revised the scheme, introducing an optional two-year extension for Agniveers not retained after four years, with higher pay, an enhanced Seva Nidhi package and a further opportunity for permanent enrolment at six years, subject to selection criteria.Uttarakhand has also introduced a 10 per cent horizontal reservation for former Agniveers in specified uniformed Group C posts, including police, fire, prisons, forest and excise services. The state has announced additional recruitment relaxations, an Agniveer employment cell and free pre-recruitment training.These measures offer the government a response to concerns about employment after military service, although their effectiveness will depend on implementation.Beyond employment, the scheme has also drawn criticism over how military service is valued. Speaking to TOI, a retired Army officer questioned the framing of military pensions as a fiscal liability and the shift towards a contractual recruitment system."You don't go places on a treadmill," the officer said.Agnipath and the battle for UttarakhandAgnipath has become politically significant in Uttarakhand because it touches several issues already shaping the state's political debate. Employment, migration, recruitment controversies and uneven development are connected by a larger question: whether young people can build a secure future in the state.That is where the opposition sees an opening.The BJP is entering the 2027 Assembly elections with an ambitious target of winning more than 60 seats, seeking a third consecutive term in a state where it has already broken the pattern of governments changing every five years.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();Speaking to TOI, Uttarakhand Congress chief spokesperson Garima Mehra Dasauni questioned the Centre's handling of Agnipath and its implications for the state's youth.“Why did defence minister Rajnath Singh remain a silent spectator when the young men of Uttarakhand were having their dreams crushed by schemes like the Agnipath scheme,” she said.Dasauni argued that the consequences of Agnipath extend beyond recruits to their families and communities, where military service has traditionally offered financial stability. She also questioned the differences between the entitlements of regular soldiers and Agniveers, including pensions, medical facilities and other benefits.“There are so many loopholes in this scheme,” she added.For Congress, Agnipath offers an opportunity to connect its criticism of the recruitment model with broader concerns over employment and social security. The party has demanded the scheme's rollback, arguing that young people need permanent military employment.The BJP, meanwhile, has a response in the Centre's November revision of Agnipath and the Uttarakhand government's reservation and employment measures for former Agniveers. These allow the party to highlight steps taken to address concerns while retaining the scheme's central objectives.As the election approaches, the debate is likely to centre not just on the recruitment model itself, but also on whether the revised provisions and employment measures deliver the opportunities promised to young recruits.The real test: Jobs, promises and the road to 2027The real test of Agnipath's political significance will lie not just in the promises made by political parties, but in how the revised scheme affects those who have served under it.As the first batches of Agniveers approach the end of their initial service periods, the Centre's revised provisions and Uttarakhand government's employment measures will face their first test. Their implementation, particularly the opportunities available to those seeking permanent military service or civilian employment, could influence the debate ahead of the elections.For the BJP, this presents an opportunity to demonstrate that the changes have addressed concerns surrounding the scheme. For Congress, it provides grounds to examine whether the measures go far enough in ensuring employment security.In a state with generations of military tradition, the debate over Agnipath is therefore likely to extend beyond recruitment policy to questions of employment, opportunity and the future of its youth.As Uttarakhand prepares to vote in 2027, Agnipath will face its own political 'agnipariksha'.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A New York man's family won a $100 million jury verdict over his death in county jail, later reduced to $20 million; appeals judges have now erased the damages and ordered a new trial on the amount
articles.summary: A family's fight for compensation over a man's death inside a New York county jail has been sent back to trial after an appeals court cancelled the
articles.body: A family's fight for compensation over a man's death inside a New York county jail has been sent back to trial after an appeals court cancelled the damages awarded in the case. The family had initially secured a $100 million jury verdict, which was later reduced to $20 million. The latest ruling has overturned that amount as well, leaving a new jury to decide the compensation for the claims that remain.The November 13 decision by New York's Appellate Division, Fourth Department, followed appeals by Erie County and five sheriff's deputies over their liability for Richard Metcalf Jr's death in 2012. The court retained claims that the deputies used excessive force against him and that one deputy failed to ensure he received adequate medical care. However, it dismissed claims against the county over the mental health care provided to Metcalf.According to the ruling available on the New York State Law Reporting Bureau's website, the case concerns Metcalf's treatment at the Erie County Holding Center, where he was restrained by deputies while awaiting medical attention. Emergency medical technicians (EMTs) later found that a spit mask had tightened around his neck. He suffered cardiac arrest and never regained consciousness. His father, Richard Metcalf Sr, subsequently filed a lawsuit against the county and the deputies involved.How the incident unfoldedMetcalf was arrested in November 2012 after breaking into a business. Police officers were told by his girlfriend that he had been behaving unusually for several days. At his court appearance the next morning, a judge ordered a mental health examination because of concerns about his behaviour.He was transferred to the holding centre, where deputies used physical force to restrain him during admission. He was later taken to Erie County Medical Center for an evaluation. After returning to the facility, a psychiatric assessment identified polysubstance dependence and recommended a follow-up examination.His condition worsened later that evening. Metcalf repeatedly struck his head against the walls and bars of his cell, injured himself with a plastic fork and smeared blood around the room. Deputies restrained him and took him to the infirmary.He was kept face down with his hands handcuffed behind his back. A spit mask was placed over his face because he was spitting blood. Staff decided to arrange another hospital evaluation.Before the EMTs arrived, Metcalf apparently chewed through the mask. Deputies said a replacement was not readily available, so they placed a pillowcase over his head without removing the damaged mask.The EMTs said they were instructed to maintain his position during the transfer. They could examine his head only after reaching the ambulance. They then noticed that his face was "cherry red" and that the spit mask had tightened around his neck. By that time, he had suffered cardiac arrest. He died at the medical centre a few days later.Appeals court retains claims against deputiesThe jury in the February 2024 trial found the county and individual deputies liable under federal civil rights law and state negligence law. However, the appeals court ruled that the evidence did not establish that the county itself had maintained a policy or practice responsible for violating Metcalf's rights.The judges noted that Metcalf had received a psychiatric assessment within 24 hours of arriving at the holding centre. Even if the examination had failed to identify his acute symptoms, the family had not established that this resulted from a county-wide policy of ignoring mental health care problems.The court also dismissed the state negligence claim against the county because the family's amended notice of claim had not specifically raised concerns about inadequate medical or psychiatric care.However, the judges allowed the excessive-force claims against all five deputies, Robert Dee, Matthew Cross, Edward Kawalek, Robert States and Scott Emerling, to continue.They found that although Metcalf had initially been difficult to restrain, testimony indicated that he was under control before the EMTs arrived. The deputies continued to keep him face down, handcuffed and covered by the mask and pillowcase.A separate negligence claim against Dee also survived. As the commanding deputy, he had personally dealt with the EMTs during the transfer. The court found that his refusal to allow them access to Metcalf's head and his rejection of safer transport arrangements exposed him to an unreasonable risk of serious harm.The negligence claims against Cross, Kawalek and States were dismissed. The medical-care claim against Emerling had also been dismissed earlier.Why the $20 million award was cancelledThe appeals court found that the jury's verdict form contained overlapping questions about Metcalf's suffering. Jurors were asked twice to calculate his pain and suffering during his time at the holding centre. Both questions covered the same period, and the jury awarded $15 million under each. The form did not clearly explain the distinction between the legal claims involved.Other questions about his suffering and fear of impending death also covered overlapping periods. The judges said this created a risk of awarding compensation more than once for the same injuries.The court therefore cancelled the entire damages award and ordered a new trial limited to the claims that survived the appeal.It also removed damages for loss of enjoyment of life after death, ruling that New York law did not permit such compensation. Punitive damages against the deputies were cancelled because the majority found insufficient evidence of the level of deliberate wrongdoing required for such an award.Judge Ogden disagreed with parts of the decision. The dissenting judge believed the county should remain liable and that punitive damages against the deputies should be retained.The court also cancelled the attorneys' fees awarded under federal civil rights law because the family's lawyers had not submitted the required records of their work.Family plans to challenge the rulingAccording to Hoodline's November 21 report, the family's lawyers intend to challenge the appellate decision and seek a review by New York's highest court.The report also said Erie County Executive Mark Poloncarz indicated that the county could still face financial responsibility for damages awarded on the surviving claims, depending on the interpretation of the ruling. The appeals court has not announced a date for the new trial.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Blink-182 bassist Mark Hoppus wins Beverly Hills tree-view lawsuit, but says neighbour still owes him $655,577 in legal fees; unpaid bill has grown to nearly $681,000 with interest
articles.summary: The Blink-182 bassist Mark Hoppus won his court fight over neighbouring trees blocking the view from his Beverly Hills home, but says his neighbour has
articles.body: The Blink-182 bassist Mark Hoppus won his court fight over neighbouring trees blocking the view from his Beverly Hills home, but says his neighbour has still not paid the $655,000 in legal fees she was ordered to cover. With interest added, the bill has grown to nearly $681,000. His lawyers have now filed a writ of execution, a court document that allows collection measures against eligible assets. The neighbour, Connie Chein, was also directed to retain a geotechnical engineer to evaluate slope stability on the hillside and recommend measures for erosion control, revegetation and soil movement.What the court ordered Mark Hoppus’ neighbour to do about the trees blocking the Hoppus family's viewAccording to TMZ, which obtained the new legal documents, Hoppus and his wife won their lawsuit in February, and the neighbour was ordered to trim or remove certain trees that the musician said were blocking their view. The judge signed off on the ruling in June, ordering landscaping changes and awarding Hoppus his attorney fees.Hoppus first sued in June 2023, claiming that the neighbour was breaking the planning commission's rules by allowing the trees to grow so tall that they blocked his view.Trousdale Estates rules that protect hillside views and the five trees at the centre of the disputeLaw Commentary reports that Hoppus and his wife, Skye, sought to enforce a Beverly Hills Planning Commission decision requiring corrective landscaping under the city's Trousdale Estates View Restoration Ordinance. The commission identified five trees that substantially interfered with the couple's view of the Los Angeles Basin once they exceeded 15 feet in height. It also found that Hoppus had substantially complied with the required outreach and mediation procedures before seeking formal intervention.The rules protect qualifying views from properties in Trousdale Estates, a hillside neighbourhood known for its panoramic views of Los Angeles. They allow homeowners to seek restrictions on neighbouring foliage that substantially obstructs those views, including through decisions requiring trees to be trimmed or removed. The dispute then reached Los Angeles Superior Court, which granted a permanent injunction requiring corrective action on the obstructing trees.How the $680,941.57 total is calculated as Hoppus's lawyers press for payment of the judgmentIn August, the court ordered Chein to provide $926,817.88 in security as a condition of pausing enforcement of the attorney fee judgment during an appeal. The court cited concerns about her ability or willingness to pay the award later.Hoppus's attorneys filed the writ on 13 November 2026, seeking $680,941.57 in total. That sum is made up of about $655,577 in court-awarded attorney fees and $25,323 in interest that accrued after the judgment went unpaid. Their filing maintains that the judgment remains unpaid.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Time to quit': Former chief of staff calls on Pete Hegseth to step down, slams Pentagon leadership
articles.summary: Former Chief of Staff Joe Kasper urges US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to resign, citing leadership failures and mismanagement of the war in Iran. Kasper's criticism highlights Hegseth's prioritization of personal image over military responsibilities.
articles.body: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is facing calls to step down from his former chief of staff, Joe Kasper, who has accused him of weakening the Pentagon's leadership, mishandling the war in Iran and prioritising his public image over the responsibilities of his office.Kasper, who worked as Hegseth's chief of staff during the first three months of the Trump administration, said the secretary's ability to lead the department was deteriorating and questioned whether he could remain effective in the position.“Pete’s ability to be effective has been constrained and very soon he’ll have lost any ability to be effective,” Kasper told POLITICO in an interview. “For that reason and others it’s time for Pete to call it quits.”During the nearly hour-long conversation, Kasper criticised Hegseth's decisions on military leadership, his approach to running the department and his conduct during the ongoing conflict with Iran.He described the administration's handling of the war as a “shitshow” and questioned the secretary's decision to remove several senior military officials. His criticism also extended to the departures of Black and female officers from senior positions in the armed forces.Kasper accused his former boss of allowing personal ambitions to take precedence over the institution he was appointed to lead.“Pete’s been belligerent in his stewardship of an office that will outlive him or any memory of his service,” he told POLITICO.His remarks come amid wider scrutiny of Hegseth's leadership and his relationship with lawmakers. Kasper claimed the defence secretary had damaged his standing on Capitol Hill, warning that the consequences could quickly affect his ability to carry out his responsibilities.“He’s not just burned bridges up on [Capitol] Hill,” Kasper said. “He’s napalmed them.”Hegseth has continued to receive backing from President Donald Trump. The defence secretary also survived an impeachment attempt earlier this month, although Democrats are expected to pursue further investigations when the new Congress convenes in January.Kasper left his position at the Pentagon in April 2025 after serving as Hegseth's chief of staff.You use AI every day.
